---
title: "Risk Measures Beyond Variance"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Risk Measures Beyond Variance"
  description-meta: "Coherent risk measures, expected shortfall as a linear program, and what replacing variance changes in a long-only allocation with PortfolioAnalytics."
---



Every optimizer in @sec-09-mean-variance-theory measured risk by the variance
of the portfolio, and nothing in the data required it: @markowitz1959 himself
proposed the semi-variance, which counts only the returns below the mean, as
the measure an investor who fears losses rather than dispersion should prefer.
@artzner1999 turned the question around and asked which properties a number
must have before it can be called a measure of risk at all, and found that the
industry's standard, value at risk, lacks the one that matters most for
building portfolios. This chapter asks what changes when variance is replaced
by a measure that has that property.

We first set out the coherence axioms, value at risk and why it fails them,
expected shortfall and the linear program that makes it as easy to optimize as
variance, its Cornish-Fisher extension, and the downside and drawdown measures
that sit beside them; then show which of these `PortfolioAnalytics` can solve,
with which solver, and where its defaults do something other than what the
specification says; then solve one long-only problem on the sixteen class
series under four objectives and read what each bought. The allocation is
**strategic** in the sense of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory:
full-sample moments, no timing, and the out-of-sample check read from the
register of @sec-25-backtesting-application rather than recomputed.

The data are the sixteen risky class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, in excess of the Treasury bill for
the reasons of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory, loaded as
@sec-09-mean-variance-theory loads them.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re), length(rf) == nrow(R))
```
:::




## Coherence, Tails, and What Variance Assumes {#sec-10-risk-measures-theory}

### Four properties of a risk measure

Write $X$ for the random excess return of a position over one period and
$\rho(X)$ for the number a risk measure assigns to it, in the units of a loss.
@artzner1999 call $\rho$ **coherent** if it satisfies four axioms:
monotonicity, so that a position which pays at least as much as another in
every state is not riskier; translation invariance, so that adding a sure
amount $c$ reduces the measured risk by exactly $c$; positive homogeneity, so
that $\rho(\lambda X) = \lambda\rho(X)$ for $\lambda > 0$; and
**subadditivity**,

$$
\rho(X + Y) \;\leq\; \rho(X) + \rho(Y).
$$ {#eq-10-subadditive}

The last axiom is the one that matters here. It says that combining two
positions can never make the measured risk larger than the sum of the two
measured separately, which is what diversification means; a measure that
violates it can rank a diversified portfolio as riskier than its concentrated
parts, and an optimizer built on it will act on that ranking. Variance is not
coherent, since it scales with $\lambda^2$ rather than $\lambda$, and the
standard deviation fails monotonicity. They are used anyway because, when
returns are elliptical, every translation-invariant and positively homogeneous
measure is an increasing function of the standard deviation at a given mean
[@mcneil2015], so the choice of measure changes no ranking. Whether returns
are elliptical is a question @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation
answered for this market: they are not.

### Value at risk

The **value at risk** at level $\alpha$ is the loss that is exceeded with
probability $\alpha$: writing $q_\alpha(X)$ for the $\alpha$-quantile of the
return,

$$
\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha(X) = -\,q_\alpha(X),
$$ {#eq-10-var}

with $\alpha = 0.05$ for the 95% level that this chapter uses throughout, and
which `PortfolioAnalytics` writes as `p = 0.95`. It is the regulatory standard
of @jorion2007; it is monotone, translation invariant and homogeneous; and it
fails @eq-10-subadditive [@artzner1999; @acerbi2002], not only in contrived
examples: a quantile ignores everything beyond itself, so two positions whose
losses each sit inside the 5% tail can, combined, produce a loss outside it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: where value at risk fails subadditivity on this data

@eq-10-subadditive can be tested on every pair of the sixteen series. For an
equally weighted pair, homogeneity turns the axiom into
$\rho\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}X + \tfrac{1}{2}Y\right) \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\rho(X) + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho(Y)$,
which is one comparison per pair. `PerformanceAnalytics` reports both as
negative numbers by default; `invert = FALSE` returns the loss as a positive
one, the convention of @eq-10-var.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
loss_var <- function(x) as.numeric(VaR(x, p = 0.95, method = "historical", invert = FALSE))
loss_es  <- function(x) as.numeric(ES(x,  p = 0.95, method = "historical", invert = FALSE))

pairs <- utils::combn(colnames(Re), 2)
mix <- apply(pairs, 2, function(p) {
  a <- as.numeric(Re[, p[1]]); b <- as.numeric(Re[, p[2]]); m <- (a + b) / 2
  c(var_mix = loss_var(m), var_avg = (loss_var(a) + loss_var(b)) / 2,
    es_mix  = loss_es(m),  es_avg  = (loss_es(a)  + loss_es(b))  / 2)
}) |>
  t() |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::mutate(a = pairs[1, ], b = pairs[2, ],
                var_fails = var_mix > var_avg + 1e-12,
                es_fails  = es_mix  > es_avg  + 1e-12)

c(pairs = nrow(mix), var_violations = sum(mix$var_fails), es_violations = sum(mix$es_fails))
#>          pairs var_violations  es_violations 
#>            120              3              0
mix |> dplyr::filter(var_fails) |> dplyr::select(a, b, var_mix, var_avg)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   a         b             var_mix var_avg
#>   <chr>     <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 CH_credit CH_government  0.0449  0.0441
#> 2 EU_credit EU_government  0.0467  0.0457
#> 3 US_credit US_government  0.0225  0.0223
```
:::




Value at risk fails on 3 of the 120 pairs,
`CH_credit` with `CH_government`, `EU_credit` with `EU_government`, and `US_credit` with `US_government`,
each a credit series combined with the government bond of its own currency.
Expected shortfall, defined below, fails on none. The
violations are small, at most
0.10 percentage points
of monthly loss, because at a 5% tail on
372 months most pairs are close to elliptical, and they are exactly
where @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application located the non-normality of
this market: in credit.
:::

### Expected shortfall and the linear program

The **expected shortfall** at level $\alpha$ is the expected loss given that
the loss exceeds the value at risk, @eq-04-es of
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-theory, also called conditional value at risk and
expected tail loss; `PortfolioAnalytics` accepts all three names. It is
coherent [@acerbi2002] and the smallest coherent measure that dominates value
at risk at the same level, which is why it is the tail measure this book uses.

What made expected shortfall usable in an optimizer is a representation due to
@rockafellar2000. For a portfolio $\boldsymbol{w}$ with return
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}$,

$$
\mathrm{ES}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{w})
= \min_{\zeta \in \mathbb{R}}
  \left\{\, \zeta + \frac{1}{\alpha}\,
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(-\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r} - \zeta\right)_+\right] \right\},
$$ {#eq-10-ru}

where $(x)_+ = \max(x, 0)$, and the minimizing $\zeta$ is the value at risk.
The expression inside the braces is convex in $(\boldsymbol{w}, \zeta)$
jointly, so minimizing it over both at once minimizes the expected shortfall
over $\boldsymbol{w}$ without ever computing a quantile. With the expectation
replaced by the average over $T$ observed return vectors
$\boldsymbol{r}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{r}_T$ and one auxiliary variable $z_t$
per observation, the minimum-ES problem under full investment and no short
sales is the linear program

$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{w},\,\zeta,\,\boldsymbol{z}} \;
  \zeta + \frac{1}{\alpha T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} z_t
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
  z_t \geq -\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}_t - \zeta,\;
  z_t \geq 0,\;
  \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,\;
  \boldsymbol{w} \geq \boldsymbol{0},
$$ {#eq-10-lp}

with $N + T + 1$ variables, here 389, and one
inequality per month. @rockafellar2002 extend the representation to
distributions with atoms, which the empirical distribution is. Every
constraint in @eq-10-lp is linear, so the problem is convex and a local minimum
is the global one [@boyd2004], as for the quadratic program of @eq-09-problem;
@sec-13-solvers-theory is about that distinction. A mean-ES frontier adds the
row $\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} \geq \bar{\mu}$ and traces $\bar{\mu}$,
and the ratio of mean excess return to expected shortfall, which the package
calls STARR, is the tail analog of the Sharpe ratio, maximized by the same
normalization that turns the maximum-Sharpe problem into a quadratic program in
@sec-13-solvers-theory.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the expected shortfall of `US_credit` by hand

The sample version of @eq-04-es is an average over the tail. With $T$ months
and $\alpha = 0.05$ the tail holds the $\alpha T$ worst observations, which is
not an integer, and `PerformanceAnalytics` averages every return strictly below
the $\alpha$-quantile.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x  <- as.numeric(Re[, "US_credit"])
q  <- stats::quantile(x, 0.05)              # the quantile; its negative is the VaR
tail_months <- x[x < q]
es_hand <- -mean(tail_months)

stopifnot(all.equal(es_hand, loss_es(x)))
c(months = length(x), alpha_T = 0.05 * length(x), in_tail = length(tail_months),
  VaR = as.numeric(-q), ES = es_hand,
  ES_modified = as.numeric(ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "modified", invert = FALSE)))
#>      months     alpha_T     in_tail         VaR          ES ES_modified 
#>   372.00000    18.60000    19.00000     0.02509     0.04470     0.09405
```
:::


The 19 months below the quantile run from
-16.4% to
-2.5%, and

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{ES}}_{0.05}
= -\frac{1}{19}\sum_{t \in \text{tail}} r_t
= -\frac{-0.8493}{19}
= 0.0447,
$$

against a value at risk of 0.0251: the average month in the
tail loses 1.8 times the loss at its edge. The
Cornish-Fisher figure of 0.0941
is the estimate @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation reported as
roughly twice the historical one, and the two disagree because the
excess-return skewness of -1.36 pushes
the expansion further out than 19 observed months reach.
:::

### The modified expected shortfall

The historical estimator uses $\alpha T$ observations, 18.6 of
them here, and @yamai2005 show that expected shortfall is estimated with a
larger standard error than value at risk from the same sample precisely because
it depends on the few observations beyond the quantile. The alternative of
@favre2002 and @boudt2008 replaces the sample tail by a normal quantile
corrected for skewness and kurtosis through the Cornish-Fisher expansion,
@eq-04-cornish-fisher, and the resulting **modified expected shortfall** is a
function of the portfolio's first four moments. Each is a polynomial in
$\boldsymbol{w}$ through the coskewness and cokurtosis tensors that
@sec-11-higher-moments-theory sets out, so the modified measure responds to
the asymmetry of every asset and every pair, and @boudt2008 also decompose it
into the contribution of each position, which is the quantity
@sec-14-risk-based-allocation-theory budgets. But it is not convex in
$\boldsymbol{w}$, and no linear program computes its minimum.
`PortfolioAnalytics` reaches it by search, which
@sec-10-risk-measures-implementation shows and @sec-13-solvers-application
measures. One default from @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation carries
over: `ES()` in `PerformanceAnalytics` returns this modified figure unless
`method = "historical"` is asked for.

### Downside measures, drawdowns, and two more coherent measures

Three further families deserve a place. The oldest is the safety-first
criterion of @roy1952, which minimizes the probability of falling below a
disaster level, and the semi-variance of @markowitz1959, which @bawa1977
generalized to the **lower partial moment** of order $n$ around a target
$\tau$,

$$
\mathrm{LPM}_n(\tau) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\tau - \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r}\right)_+^{\,n}\right],
$$ {#eq-10-lpm}

whose square root at $n = 2$ is the downside deviation and the denominator of
the ratio of @sortino1991. Drawdown measures ask about the path rather than
the distribution: @chekhlov2005 define the conditional drawdown at risk as the
average of the worst $\alpha$ share of drawdowns and show that it, too, is
minimized by a linear program of the form of @eq-10-lp, with drawdowns in
place of losses. The third family is the one @krokhmal2007 built by replacing
the average in @eq-10-ru with a higher norm. At the second order,

$$
\mathrm{CSM}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{w})
= \min_{\zeta}
  \left\{\, \zeta + \frac{1}{\alpha}\,
  \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(-\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{r} - \zeta\right)_+^{2}\right]} \right\},
$$ {#eq-10-csm}

which is coherent, penalizes the shape of the tail beyond its average, and is
a second-order cone program rather than a linear one; `PortfolioAnalytics`
names it `CSM`. The package also offers `EQS`, an "expected quadratic
shortfall" documented only by its code, which minimizes over $\zeta$ the
expression of @eq-10-ru with a squared positive part in place of the loss;
which tail it squares is a question @sec-10-risk-measures-implementation
measures rather than assumes.

### What the choice of measure assumes

Each measure encodes a belief about what the investor of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory dislikes. Variance treats a gain
of ten percent and a loss of ten percent as the same event, and by
@eq-03-quadratic-utility that is right only if utility is quadratic or every
higher moment is a function of the first two, the two cases @markowitz1959
identified; @levy1979 and @markowitz2014 find the approximation good across
most utility functions and return histories, and poor where returns are far
from normal. A tail measure asks about one side of the distribution only, and
so responds to skewness and kurtosis, which
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application showed to live in credit rather than
in equity: `US_credit` has the third-best Sharpe ratio of the sixteen and
a total-return skewness of
-1.45, the most negative of them. Markets appear
to price downside risk separately from variance [@ang2006], so the choice is
not only a matter of taste; and it has a cost in estimation, since the
historical tail uses a twentieth of the sample and the modified one inherits
the sample skewness, which @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation found to
change sign in a third of rolling windows. @sec-11-higher-moments-theory takes
the comoments as inputs; here they enter only through the measure.

One rule from @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory governs what follows:
the measure a portfolio is judged by must be the measure it was chosen by, and
a comparison across objectives has to show every portfolio on every measure so
that the mismatch is visible. @sec-10-risk-measures-application does that.

## Implementation {#sec-10-risk-measures-implementation}

### The objectives the package knows

A risk objective in `PortfolioAnalytics` is named for the function that
computes it. `"var"` or `"StdDev"` is the variance of @eq-09-moments;
`"ES"`, with the aliases `"ETL"` and `"CVaR"`, is @eq-04-es, taking its level
and estimator as `arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "historical")`;
`"VaR"` is @eq-10-var, which no convex solver accepts, since a quantile is not
convex in the weights, so it is reachable only through the search methods of
@sec-13-solvers-theory; `"CSM"` and `"EQS"` are solved by `CVXR` only. Four
specifications on one constraint set carry the chapter: minimum variance,
minimum historical expected shortfall, quadratic utility at
`risk_aversion = 2`, which by the $\gamma/2$ convention of
@sec-91-proofs-quadratic-utility is $\gamma = 4$, and minimum modified expected
shortfall.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

spec_var <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
spec_es  <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES",
                                       arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "historical"))
spec_mes <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES",
                                       arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "modified"))
spec_qu  <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = 2)   # lambda = 2, i.e. gamma = 4
```
:::


The first three are convex and go to `ROI`: a quadratic program for the two
variance objectives, as in @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, and the linear
program of @eq-10-lp for the shortfall.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w_of <- function(opt) extractWeights(opt)[colnames(Re)]      # always index by name

o_var <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_var, optimize_method = "ROI")
o_es  <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_es,  optimize_method = "ROI")
o_qu  <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_qu,  optimize_method = "ROI")
w_var <- w_of(o_var); w_es <- w_of(o_es); w_qu <- w_of(o_qu)
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_es) - 1) < 1e-6, all(w_es >= -1e-8))

W3   <- rbind(`minimum variance` = w_var, `minimum ES` = w_es, `quadratic utility` = w_qu)
keep <- colnames(Re)[apply(W3, 2, max) > 0.005]
round(W3[, keep], 3)
#>                   EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity JP_equity JP_government UK_equity
#> minimum variance      0.014            0.051     0.042         0.000     0.022
#> minimum ES            0.000            0.044     0.021         0.019     0.039
#> quadratic utility     0.312            0.000     0.000         0.000     0.000
#>                   US_credit US_equity US_government
#> minimum variance      0.000     0.051         0.821
#> minimum ES            0.000     0.029         0.849
#> quadratic utility     0.098     0.589         0.000
```
:::


The risk numbers come back two ways. `extractObjectiveMeasures()` reports what
the solver minimized, and `extract_risk()` recomputes the mean, the standard
deviation and all three tail measures for any weight vector, so a portfolio
chosen by one measure can be read on the others.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
extractObjectiveMeasures(o_es)
#> $ES
#> [1] 0.02394
unlist(extract_risk(Re, w_es)[c("StdDev", "ES", "CSM")])
#>  StdDev      ES     CSM 
#> 0.01215 0.02394 0.03516
```
:::


The two `ES` figures agree, and both are the value of @eq-10-lp, which with
$\alpha T = 18.6$ interpolates between the eighteenth and
nineteenth worst months, rather than the sample-tail average of `ES()`; the
two differ at the fourth decimal,
0.0239 against
0.0238.

::: {.callout-note}
## Under `ROI` the `method` argument is not read

The linear program of @eq-10-lp is the sample formulation, and it is the only
formulation `ROI` has. Asking for `method = "modified"` on an `ES` objective
and then solving with `ROI` returns the historical solution without a message.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
o_mes_roi <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mes, optimize_method = "ROI")
c(same_weights_as_historical = isTRUE(all.equal(w_of(o_mes_roi), w_es)))
#> same_weights_as_historical 
#>                       TRUE
```
:::


The modified measure needs a solver that evaluates the objective as a black
box, which means differential evolution [@storn1997; @ardia2011], particle
swarm, simulated annealing or random portfolios, none of which carries an
optimality guarantee. We use differential evolution with a small budget, and
@sec-10-risk-measures-application shows what the budget bought.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)
invisible(utils::capture.output(
  o_mes <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mes, optimize_method = "DEoptim",
                              search_size = 2000, itermax = 50, traceDE = 0)
))
w_mes <- w_of(o_mes)
c(modified_ES = as.numeric(extractObjectiveMeasures(o_mes)$ES),
  US_credit = w_mes[["US_credit"]], positions = sum(w_mes > 0.005),
  seconds = round(as.numeric(o_mes$elapsed_time, units = "secs"), 1))
#> modified_ES   US_credit   positions     seconds 
#>     0.02546     0.01200     9.00000    19.90000
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## A mean plus a risk objective is a ratio problem by default, but only for the tail measures

`optimize.portfolio()` decides what one return objective plus one risk
objective means, and decides differently for different measures. With `mean`
and `StdDev` the default `maxSR = FALSE` makes it a quadratic-utility problem
at the default `risk_aversion = 1`, and the tangency portfolio needs
`maxSR = TRUE`. With `mean` and `ES` the default is `maxSTARR = TRUE`, as it
is for `CSMratio` and `EQSratio`: the package maximizes the ratio unless told
not to, and `maxSTARR = FALSE` turns the specification into a minimum-ES
problem in which the return objective is merely reported.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_mean_es <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95))
spec_mean_sd <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

starr  <- function(w) { x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w); mean(x) / loss_es(x) }
sharpe <- function(w) { x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w); mean(x) / stats::sd(x) }

asked <- list(
  `mean + ES, defaults`         = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_es, optimize_method = "ROI"),
  `mean + ES, maxSTARR = FALSE` = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_es, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                                     maxSTARR = FALSE),
  `mean + StdDev, defaults`     = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_sd, optimize_method = "ROI"),
  `mean + StdDev, maxSR = TRUE` = optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_sd, optimize_method = "ROI",
                                                     maxSR = TRUE)
)

# What each default actually solved, checked rather than asserted.
w_qu1 <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = 1), optimize_method = "ROI"))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(w_of(asked[[2]]), w_es,  tolerance = 1e-4)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(w_of(asked[[3]]), w_qu1, tolerance = 1e-4)))

ratios <- tibble::tibble(
  specification = names(asked),
  solves  = c("maximum STARR", "minimum ES", "quadratic utility, risk_aversion = 1",
              "maximum Sharpe"),
  STARR   = vapply(asked, function(o) starr(w_of(o)),  numeric(1)),
  Sharpe  = vapply(asked, function(o) sharpe(w_of(o)), numeric(1)),
  largest = vapply(asked, function(o) {
    w <- w_of(o); sprintf("%s %.0f%%", names(which.max(w)), 100 * max(w)) }, character(1))
)
```
:::



::: {#tbl-10-ratio-defaults .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Four two-objective specifications and what each solved. STARR is the monthly mean excess return over the 95% expected shortfall; the Sharpe ratio is monthly.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}

|:---------------------------|:------------------------------------|-----:|------:|:-----------------|
|mean + ES, defaults         |maximum STARR                        | 0.138|  0.282|US_government 70% |
|mean + ES, maxSTARR = FALSE |minimum ES                           | 0.103|  0.203|US_government 85% |
|mean + StdDev, defaults     |quadratic utility, risk_aversion = 1 | 0.093|  0.214|EU_equity 52%     |
|mean + StdDev, maxSR = TRUE |maximum Sharpe                       | 0.137|  0.286|US_government 68% |

The two default rows of @tbl-10-ratio-defaults have
27% of their weight in common: one maximizes a
tail ratio and holds mostly `US_government`, the other a utility whose risk
penalty is almost switched off and holds only equity,
`EU_equity` first. Nothing in the
returned object says
which was solved beyond the name of the objective measure. State the ratio
arguments explicitly in every call, in both directions.
:::

### The mean-ES frontier

`create.EfficientFrontier()` with `type = "mean-ETL"` calls
`meanetl.efficient.frontier()`, which solves @eq-10-lp for the minimum-ES
portfolio, for the maximum return, and then for `n.portfolios` return targets
between them. `chart.EfficientFrontier()` draws it in one call, its default
`match.col = "ES"` locating the horizontal axis; the mean-variance frontier of
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation is computed beside it on the same
constraints.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ef_es <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, spec_mean_es, type = "mean-ETL",
                                  n.portfolios = 50, optimize_method = "ROI")
ef_sd <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, spec_mean_sd, type = "mean-StdDev",
```

```{.r .cell-code}
weights_of <- function(fr) {
  W <- as.matrix(fr[, grep("^w[.]", colnames(fr))])

                 w_credit = W[, "US_credit"])

)
pts <- dplyr::bind_rows(frontier_frame(fr_es, "mean-ES frontier"),
```

```{.r .cell-code}
x_credit <- as.numeric(Re[, "US_credit"])
i_worst  <- which.min(x_credit)
d_worst  <- zoo::index(Re)[i_worst]                    # the worst month of the series
per_sd   <- function(method) apply(Re, 2, function(x)
  as.numeric(ES(as.numeric(x), p = 0.95, method = method, invert = FALSE)) / stats::sd(x))
tail_sd  <- list(historical = per_sd("historical"), modified = per_sd("modified"))
tail_rank <- vapply(tail_sd, function(v) rank(-v)[["US_credit"]], numeric(1))

credit_tail <- c(skewness            = as.numeric(skewness(x_credit)),
                 without_worst_month = as.numeric(skewness(x_credit[-i_worst])),
                 worst_month_in_sd   = (x_credit[i_worst] - mean(x_credit)) / stats::sd(x_credit),
                 ES_per_sd           = tail_sd$historical[["US_credit"]],
                 modified_ES_per_sd  = tail_sd$modified[["US_credit"]])
stopifnot(in_episode(d_worst, "credit_crisis"),
          abs(credit_tail[["without_worst_month"]]) < 0.25 * abs(credit_tail[["skewness"]]),
          tail_rank[["historical"]] > 4, tail_rank[["modified"]] <= 3)
round(credit_tail, 2)
#>            skewness without_worst_month   worst_month_in_sd           ES_per_sd 
#>               -1.36               -0.03               -8.01                2.13 
#>  modified_ES_per_sd 
#>                4.49
tail_rank
#> historical   modified 
#>          8          2
```
:::


The skewness of `US_credit` is the work of one month, October of model year 17
in the credit crisis, a return
8.0 standard deviations
below the mean: without it the excess-return skewness is
-0.03 rather than
-1.36. A 5% tail averages that month
with 18 others, so the historical expected shortfall of the series is
2.13 times its standard deviation,
rank 8 of the sixteen, where the Cornish-Fisher
figure, which is built from the skewness, is
4.49 times, rank
2. The frontier holdings that differ by so much are
separated by the few hundredths of a percentage point of risk reported above,
which is the statement of @mcneil2015 made on sixteen assets: series that are
close to elliptical are ranked the same way by both measures, and the weights
on which the two frontiers disagree are weakly determined by either.

### Two coherent measures that need a cone solver

`CSM` and `EQS` are solved by `CVXR` alone, through the formulation of
@eq-10-csm and its squared counterpart; `meancsm.efficient.frontier()` and
`meaneqs.efficient.frontier()` trace their frontiers the way
`meanetl.efficient.frontier()` does. Their minimum-risk portfolios sit beside
the minimum-ES one.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_csm <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "CSM", arguments = list(p = 0.95))
spec_eqs <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "EQS", arguments = list(p = 0.95))

w_csm <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_csm, optimize_method = "CVXR"))
w_eqs <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_eqs, optimize_method = "CVXR"))

W_tail <- rbind(`minimum ES` = w_es, `minimum CSM` = w_csm, `minimum EQS` = w_eqs)
round(W_tail[, colnames(Re)[apply(W_tail, 2, max) > 0.005]], 3)
#>             CH_equity CH_government EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity JP_equity
#> minimum ES      0.000         0.000      0.00            0.044     0.021
#> minimum CSM     0.016         0.205      0.00            0.000     0.000
#> minimum EQS     0.018         0.000      0.03            0.043     0.070
#>             JP_government UK_equity UK_government US_equity US_government
#> minimum ES          0.019     0.039         0.000     0.029         0.849
#> minimum CSM         0.000     0.030         0.000     0.090         0.660
#> minimum EQS         0.000     0.000         0.084     0.000         0.756
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## `CSM` is unavailable to the search methods

Every objective a metaheuristic evaluates passes through
`constrained_objective()`, and that function's branch for `CSM` is empty: it
sets no function, so the objective contributes nothing to the score (upstream
issue #51, recorded in @sec-93-package-notes). A random-portfolio or
differential-evolution run on a `CSM` objective does not fail; it scores every
candidate at zero and returns the first one it looked at.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)
rp <- random_portfolios(base_spec, permutations = 2000, rp_method = "simplex")
o_csm_rp <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_csm, optimize_method = "random", rp = rp, trace = TRUE)

scores <- vapply(o_csm_rp$random_portfolio_objective_results, function(z) z$out, numeric(1))
c(candidates = nrow(rp), distinct_scores = length(unique(scores)), score = unique(scores)[1],
  returned_first_candidate = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(w_of(o_csm_rp)),
                                              unname(rp[1, colnames(Re)]))))
#>               candidates          distinct_scores                    score 
#>                     1606                        1                        0 
#> returned_first_candidate 
#>                        1
length(extractObjectiveMeasures(o_csm_rp))
#> [1] 0
```
:::


The returned object has weights, an empty list of objective measures, and no
warning. Use `CVXR` for `CSM`, and treat an empty `extractObjectiveMeasures()`
as the signature of an objective that was never evaluated.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Two things to check before trusting an `EQS` number

The ratio problems are solved in a normalized form, mean fixed at one and box
and group limits scaled by the weight sum, and the weights are rescaled to sum
to one afterwards. Earlier builds skipped the rescaling, so that a box or group
limit on a ratio problem did not bind in the returned weights; on the build
recorded in @sec-93-package-notes it does, and we measure it rather than assume
it. What does not survive the rescaling is the objective value: expected
shortfall and `CSM` are homogeneous and divide through, while `EQS` is
quadratic in the weights, so the figure reported for a ratio solution is not
the `EQS` of the weights reported with it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# split() orders groups alphabetically; the limit vectors are built by name and
# the assertion fails the render if they ever drift apart.
grp  <- split(seq_len(ncol(Re)), dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", colnames(Re))     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", colnames(Re)) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", colnames(Re))     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                                ~ "commodity"))
gmin <- c(commodity = 0.00, credit = 0.05, equity = 0.20, government = 0.10)
gmax <- c(commodity = 0.15, credit = 0.40, equity = 0.60, government = 0.50)
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(gmin)), identical(names(grp), names(gmax)))

spec_eqs_ratio <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.25) |>
  add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp,
                 group_min = unname(gmin), group_max = unname(gmax)) |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "EQS", arguments = list(p = 0.95))

o_eqs_ratio <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_eqs_ratio, optimize_method = "CVXR")  # EQSratio = TRUE
w_r     <- w_of(o_eqs_ratio)
group_w <- vapply(grp, function(g) sum(w_r[g]), numeric(1))

c(sum = sum(w_r), largest = max(w_r),
  box_binds    = all(w_r <= 0.25 + 1e-6),
  groups_bind  = all(group_w >= gmin - 1e-6 & group_w <= gmax + 1e-6),
  reported_EQS = as.numeric(extractObjectiveMeasures(o_eqs_ratio)$EQS),
  EQS_of_weights = extract_risk(Re, w_r)$EQS)
#>            sum        largest      box_binds    groups_bind   reported_EQS 
#>       1.000000       0.250000       1.000000       1.000000       0.416255 
#> EQS_of_weights 
#>       0.002253
```
:::


The second check concerns the measure itself. In both `optimize.portfolio()`
and `extract_risk()` the quantity squared is the positive part of the
portfolio **return**, where the `ES` and `CSM` branches of the same functions
take the positive part of its negative. The number the package calls `EQS`
is therefore the tail average of squared gains, and only on negated returns
does it become the tail average of squared losses.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The empirical version of the minimization in @eq-10-ru for a nonnegative
# series v: the average of its largest alpha share, interpolated at the edge.
tail_mean <- function(v, alpha = 0.05) {
  v <- sort(v, decreasing = TRUE); m <- alpha * length(v); k <- floor(m)
  (sum(v[seq_len(k)]) + (m - k) * v[k + 1]) / m
}
r_es <- as.numeric(Re %*% w_es)
eqs_check <- c(package_EQS            = extract_risk(Re, w_es)$EQS,
               tail_of_squared_gains  = tail_mean(pmax(r_es, 0)^2),
               tail_of_squared_losses = tail_mean(pmax(-r_es, 0)^2),
               package_EQS_on_negated = extract_risk(-Re, w_es)$EQS)
stopifnot(all.equal(eqs_check[["package_EQS"]], eqs_check[["tail_of_squared_gains"]],
                    tolerance = 1e-3))
signif(eqs_check, 4)
#>            package_EQS  tail_of_squared_gains tail_of_squared_losses 
#>              0.0008126              0.0008126              0.0006052 
#> package_EQS_on_negated 
#>              0.0006052

skew_of <- function(w) as.numeric(skewness(as.numeric(Re %*% w)))
stopifnot(skew_of(w_eqs) < skew_of(w_es))        # the order the next sentence states
```
:::


Minimizing the package's `EQS` therefore penalizes large gains, which is why
its minimum-risk portfolio above has a more negative skewness than the
minimum-ES one, -0.44 against
-0.10. Until the sign is corrected upstream, an `EQS` objective
should be posed on `-Re`, and every `EQS` figure read from the returned
weights rather than from the returned object.
:::

## Four Objectives on One Universe {#sec-10-risk-measures-application}

### What each objective bought

The four portfolios of @sec-10-risk-measures-implementation solve the same
long-only, fully invested problem and differ only in what they call risk. Each
is reported here on every measure, with the tail measures computed on the
excess returns that were optimized and the drawdown on the total-return wealth
path.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
portfolios <- list(`minimum variance` = w_var,
                   `minimum ES` = w_es,
                   `quadratic utility, lambda = 2` = w_qu,
                   `minimum modified ES (search)` = w_mes)

measures_of <- function(w) {
  x  <- as.numeric(Re %*% w)                                       # excess, what was optimized
  xt <- xts::xts(as.numeric(R %*% w), order.by = zoo::index(R))    # total, for the wealth path
  c(US_credit = w[["US_credit"]], positions = sum(w > 0.005),
    ret = mean(x) * 12, vol = stats::sd(x) * sqrt(12),
    ES = loss_es(x),
    modified_ES = as.numeric(ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "modified", invert = FALSE)),
    utility = (mean(x) - 2 * stats::var(x)) * 12,                   # mu - lambda sigma^2, lambda = 2
    skewness = as.numeric(skewness(x)),
    max_drawdown = as.numeric(maxDrawdown(xt)))
}
four <- t(vapply(portfolios, measures_of, numeric(9))) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("portfolio")
```
:::

@tbl-10-oos, from portfolios each built on a 5% tail of 1.8
observations. A tail of two months is not an estimate of a distribution; it
is two months. @sec-25-backtesting-application puts the error bar of @lo2002
on every Sharpe ratio in the register: by @eq-25-se the standard error of
this one is 0.22, and the six Sharpe ratios of
@tbl-10-oos lie within 0.22 of one
another. Choose the measure for what it sees, report by the
measure chosen, and do not read a rank from a tail that holds two
observations.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A risk measure is coherent if it is monotone, translation invariant,
  positively homogeneous and subadditive [@artzner1999]. Value at risk fails
  subadditivity on 3 of the 120 pairs in this
  market; expected shortfall never does [@acerbi2002]; variance is not
  coherent either, but ranks portfolios correctly when returns are elliptical.
- The representation of @rockafellar2000, @eq-10-ru, turns minimum expected
  shortfall into the linear program @eq-10-lp, convex and solved exactly by
  `ROI`; the modified expected shortfall of @favre2002 and @boudt2008 depends
  on the third and fourth moments, is not convex, and is reached only by search.
- In `PortfolioAnalytics` a `mean` plus `ES`, `CSM` or `EQS` specification is
  a ratio problem unless `maxSTARR`, `CSMratio` or `EQSratio` is `FALSE`,
  while `mean` plus `StdDev` is a quadratic-utility problem unless
  `maxSR = TRUE`; `ROI` ignores `method = "modified"`; `CSM` is silently
  unevaluated by the search methods; and `EQS` squares the gains.
- On the sixteen class series the two frontiers are almost the same curve and
  not the same portfolios: at a matched return their `US_credit` weights
  differ by up to 10 percentage
  points, and in both directions. A 5% historical tail does not register the
  skewness of that series, which is the work of one month; the Cornish-Fisher
  estimate does. Of the four objectives only quadratic utility holds it in
  size, and the minimum-ES portfolio is the closest to symmetric of the convex
  solutions.
- Report each portfolio by the measure it optimized, and show all on all
  measures. Out of sample the minimum-ES rule realizes a higher expected
  shortfall than minimum variance at every window: a 5% tail on sixty months
  is three observations, and a thirty-six-month window's Sharpe ratio rests on
  two.
